newsitem.title: UK: For lira and peseta, does EMU 1999 or 2002 matter?
newsitem.headline: For lira and peseta, does EMU 1999 or 2002 matter?

text.p: While Italian and Spanish markets were rattled this week by creeping speculation about a delay in their membership of a single currency, many analysts are not convinced a three-year delay really makes much difference.

Continued commitment to fiscal and economic convergence, necessary whether members or aspiring members of the single currency, and the prospect of joining before 2002 should be enough to justify existing investment.

Moreover, analysts believe the dash to be part of the first wave of European monetary union (EMU) in 1999 is likely to have been an attempt by Italy and Spain to force France and Germany to set up concrete contingencies for their later arrival anyway.
In any event, the financial markets are not fully priced for Italy, Spain, Portugal or Sweden being members of EMU in 1999.

"The market really hasn't been fully pricing the likes of Italy and Spain in the first wave anyway and it is positioned more for their inclusion before notes and coins are issued in 2002," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.
This is partly why the market reaction to the hardening of Germany's public stance against a initial broad-based EMU has been fairly limited to date.
The lira and peseta are less than two percent weaker than this time last week and both are still stronger than their respective mid-rates in the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
Italian bonds rallied today despite a story in the Financial Times about EU plans to delay Italian and Spanish EMU entry.

Even George Soros, head of the multi-billion-dollar U.S. investment funds, said Monday that a firm committment by the EU to admit Italy, Spain and Portugal in a second wave of EMU would minimise any market impact from the exclusion from the start.
"If you have a firm committment that (they will) be in the second round, the effect of the bond market could be quite mild," he said at the World Economic Forum in Davos.
Many other analysts agree with Soros, widely reported to have made about one billion dollars for his funds in betting on sterling's exit from the ERM in 1992.
"Assuming these countries continue to meet the convergence criteria by 2001 then there's no good reason why Germany or anyone else can argue for their exclusion," said UBS's Maydell.

"EMU calculators", which are devised by markets to assess the perceived probability of countries joining EMU in 1999 by examining changes in bond yield spreads in the swaps market, point to a lingering doubt over some contestants.

They currently show that while the probability of Spain and Italy starting EMU in 1999 has risen in recent months, their chances are still only between 70 and 80 percent. This compares with a 100 percent perceived chance for France and the Benelux.

Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg, who becomes president of the European Monetary Institute this summer, said he thinks the three Benelux countries, Germany, France, Austria, Finland and Ireland will start EMU on January 1, 1999.
However, he said this week that "It's not a catastrophe if one, two, three, four countries join a little later."
Duisenberg also said he expects all 15 EU countries to join EMU by the time euro notes and coins are issued in 2002.
"Italy and Spain have been gunning for 1999 to maximise their leverage in negotiations with Germany and France," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"But, if you genuinely believe Italy and Spain will be part of EMU within five years, does it really matter whether its 1999 or 2002?" said Prendergast.

"There maybe a risk that the current fiscal squeeze will be politically destabilising in these countries, but the EU stability pact means that, in or out of EMU in 1999, the fiscal outlook for Italians is not very pleasant anyway."
Yet, other analysts said the concern about delay for these countries is the impact on domestic political and public will.

"Any more than a small administrative delay, would risk disturbing fragile political processes because of the extraordinary fiscal pressure already being demanded to make the cut on time," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro
"The question of how long you can maintain such a fiscal squeeze without the short-term political pay-off of EMU could create real internal problems," he said.
